articles.title: Fed's Beth Hammack and Thomas Barkin favour gradual rate hikes as inflation stays high
articles.summary: Federal Reserve officials Beth Hammack and Thomas Barkin are making the case for a gradual approach to interest rate increases, signalling that policymakers remain focused on bringing inflation under control even as uncertainty over the economic outlook grows, Reuters reported.Their comments on Thursday come as the US central bank faces competing pressures from persistent price increases, geopolitical tensions and heavy investment in artificial intelligence (AI). The remarks also mark the first round of comments from Fed officials after Democrats won control of Congress and made gains in state level elections. For live updates on US Markets, click here "I expect that monetary policy will need to move to a restrictive stance to bring inflation back to 2% in a timely manner," Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack said in a speech ahead of an event in Zurich.According to Reuters, Hammack, a consistent supporter of higher borrowing costs, favours smaller and more frequent adjustments rather than sharp increases. She said this approach would be less disruptive to households, businesses and financial markets. Gradual increases could also prevent an “inflationary mindset” from taking hold, she added.Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin echoed that view, saying inflation remained “too high” and was holding firm rather than easing. "When it comes to the pace of future rate hikes, gradual makes sense," he said.Inflation keeps pressure on the FedThe comments follow the Fed's decision last week to keep its benchmark interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range. Hammack, along with Fed Governor Lisa Cook, voted in favour of a rate increase, highlighting the divide among policymakers over how aggressively to tackle inflation.Also Read: Emerging markets lose $33.8 billion in October as investors flee Asian stocksFinancial markets broadly expect another increase in December, although expectations beyond that remain less certain. Reuters reported that futures traders have lowered the probability of a December hike to around 70% from more than 80% on Wednesday.AI investment and elections add to uncertaintyThe political shift could also influence the inflation outlook. Local voter opposition to data centres and permitting challenges could slow AI infrastructure spending, potentially easing demand for equipment and related resources.Evercore ISI analysts told clients on Wednesday that AI capital expenditure could slow in the next year or two, helping keep demand and supply in balance without requiring many more rate increases.TD Securities said it expects the Fed to raise rates by another 50 basis points by early next year. However, the brokerage said a resolution to the Iran war or a slowdown in AI investment could reduce the need for further tightening after March.Meanwhile, Friday's US jobs report is expected to provide another test for policymakers, with economists forecasting 65,000 additional jobs in October after September's 29,000 gain, Reuters reported.(Disclaimer: This article is based on inputs from agencies. These do not represent the views of The Economic Times)

articles.summary: WASHINGTON: The number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment slipped to a 57-year last week as layoffs remained low against the backdrop of a resilient labor market.Initial claims for state unemployment benefits fell 6,000 to a seasonally adjusted 189,000 for the week ended October 31, the Labor Department said on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast 196,000 claims for the latest week.Claims matched the 189,000 level touched in mid-July, which was the lowest reading since 1969.They have stayed mostly below 200,000 since mid-September.Low layoffs, thanks to strong domestic demand and profit growth, are anchoring the labor market, with hiring still constrained by uncertainty over the dragging US-Israeli war with Iran.The government reported this week that there were 1.06 open jobs for every unemployed person in September, up from 1.02 in August, which some economists argued was a sign of the labor market starting to tighten. Others, however, viewed the low level of jobless claims as a function of a smaller labor force amid an immigration crackdown, rather than fewer job cuts.A separate report from global outplacement firm Challenger, Gray and Christmas on Thursday showed US-based employers announced 43,994 job cuts in October, up 2% from September. Planned layoffs dropped 71% compared to October 2025.Despite the rise over the month, layoffs were the lowest for any October since 2023. Employers announced plans to hire 444,692 workers last month, a 57% jump from October 2025. Hiring plans were the highest for any October since 2009, and likely mostly seasonal jobs."Employers are holding on to the workers they have heading into the holidays, and the hiring they are announcing is largely short-term, seasonal work," said Andy Challenger, chief revenue officer at Challenger, Gray & Christmas. "Companies want the flexibility to meet holiday demand without adding permanent headcount."The reluctance to increase permanent hiring means some unemployed people are experiencing long periods of joblessness.The claims report showed the number of people receiving unemployment benefits after an initial week of aid, a proxy for hiring, increased 23,000 to a still-low seasonally adjusted 1.718 million during the week ended October 24. The so-called continuing claims, however, do not include some unemployed people, including recent college graduates and others who have little or no work history.Some people might also have exhausted their eligibility for benefits, limited to 26 weeks in most states, keeping continuing claims at relatively low levels.The claims report has no bearing on the government's closely watched employment report for October due on Friday as it falls outside the survey period. articles.summary: Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC), the country's largest insurer, reported a nearly 20% rise in consolidated net profit to Rs 12,114.78 crore for the September quarter on Thursday, supported by strong growth in premium income and higher investment earnings. The state-owned insurer had reported a net profit of Rs 10,098 crore in the corresponding quarter last year. However, profit declined 11% sequentially from Rs 13,584 crore in the June quarter.Net premium income increased 16.2% year-on-year to Rs 1.47 lakh crore from Rs 1.26 lakh crore in the September quarter of FY26. It rose 15% sequentially from Rs 1.27 lakh crore.The growth in premium income was largely driven by a sharp increase in single-premium collections, reflecting higher contributions from policies where customers pay the entire premium upfront.Single-premium income surged 34% to Rs 68,425 crore from Rs 50,882 crore a year earlier. However, first-year premium income declined 4% to Rs 10,484 crore from Rs 10,884 crore.LIC also reported an increase in investment income during the quarter, providing additional support to profitability.Net investment income in the shareholders' account increased to Rs 2,855 crore from Rs 2,066 crore a year earlier, representing a rise of about 38%.Total income in the shareholders' account increased 11% to Rs 10,527 crore from Rs 9,454 crore. Meanwhile, the insurer's income from investments in the policyholders' account stood at Rs 1.15 lakh crore, compared with Rs 1.12 lakh crore in the year-ago quarter, an increase of around 2.2%.The company reported a surplus of Rs 10,379 crore in the policyholders' account, compared with Rs 9,503 crore a year earlier. articles.summary: New Delhi: Mehli Mistry has challenged his removal as a trustee of Sir Dorabji Tata Trust (SDTT) and Bai Hirabai Jamsetji Tata Navsari Charitable Institution before the Maharashtra Charity Commissioner, alleging procedural irregularities and violations of trust governance rules.In three rejoinders and applications filed before the Deputy Charity Commissioner, Mistry has questioned the legality of the decisions leading to his removal, the eligibility of certain trustees and their participation in decisions concerning his reappointment.He has also sought an independent inquiry into SDTT's administration, alleging conflicts of interest, improper retention of financial benefits by trustees and irregularities in decisions involving Tata Group companies and the trust's investments in Tata Sons.A key issue raised by Mistry concerns Venu Srinivasan's participation in the decision on his reappointment. Mistry has argued that Srinivasan's tenure as a trustee ended on October 23, 2025, while he communicated his vote against Mistry's reappointment on October 28.Read more: Tata Sons Chairman Chandrasekaran meets Italian PM Meloni after Iveco acquisitionAccording to Mistry, the trust's own records acknowledged that Srinivasan was no longer a trustee when he cast his vote. He has pointed out that a footnote in the records stated that Srinivasan's vote should be disregarded for this reason.However, Mistry contends that removing the vote from the final count does not address the larger issue, as Srinivasan was still included in the decision-making process. He has argued that the entire resolution was invalid because the body considering his reappointment was not properly constituted.Mistry has also disputed the trust's position that his three-year tenure ended on October 28, 2025, requiring a fresh resolution for reappointment. He has cited the SDTT Trust Deed of March 11, 1932, arguing that it does not prescribe a fixed tenure for trustees.He has further relied on an October 17, 2024, joint resolution of SDTT and Sir Ratan Tata Trust, which provided for the reappointment of trustees after the expiry of their tenure without any limitation on the renewed term, subject to applicable law.Read more: Finance Minister Sitharaman urges Tata to resolve feud amicably, rules out govt interventionIn a separate challenge concerning the Bai Hirabai Jamsetji Tata Navsari Charitable Institution, Mistry has questioned the eligibility of trustees under the trust deed. He has cited provisions requiring trustees to profess the Parsi Zoroastrian faith and meet specified residency conditions.On this basis, he has questioned the eligibility of Venu Srinivasan and Vijay Singh. He has also raised questions about Noel Tata's alleged Irish citizenship and UAE residency, arguing that eligibility requirements should be applied uniformly to all trustees.Mistry has sought affidavits from trustees confirming that they meet the qualifications prescribed under the trust deed. He has also disputed the trust's position that the relevant eligibility provisions are invalid or unenforceable.Separately, Mistry has sought an inquiry into the financial affairs of SDTT, particularly commissions and other benefits allegedly received by trustees serving as nominee directors in Tata Group companies.His application refers to an annual commission of approximately Rs 1.42 crore received by Noel Tata from Tata Sons Private Limited during FY 2024-25, as reflected in corporate filings.He has also raised questions concerning the engagement of Gerry McGovern for Norton Motorcycles, equity infusion into Tata International Limited and alleged deviations from unanimous resolutions on voting the trust's shareholding in Tata Sons.Mistry has argued that such matters could involve conflicts of interest and breaches of fiduciary duties. articles.title: Bharti Airtel Q2 Results: Net profit jumps 31% YoY to Rs 8,887 crore; revenue up 17%; ARPU rises to Rs 271
articles.summary: Bharti Airtel reported a 31% year-on-year (YoY) increase in net profit to Rs 8,887.5 crore for the September quarter (Q2FY27), compared with Rs 6,791.6 crore in the corresponding quarter last fiscal.The telecom major's consolidated revenue for the quarter rose 16.7% YoY to Rs 60,878 crore, up from Rs 52,145 crore reported in Q2FY26.India mobile revenue grew 10.1% YoY, while ARPU increased to Rs 271 in Q2FY27 from Rs 256 in the year-ago quarter, reflecting improved customer realisations.Operating performance remained strong, with earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) growing 17.8% YoY to Rs 35,240 crore in Q2FY27, compared with Rs 29,919 crore in the year-ago period.India revenue increased 9.4% YoY to Rs 42,308 crore, with the company's mobile business continuing to benefit from premiumisation of its customer portfolio, higher average revenue per user (ARPU) and strong additions in smartphone data customers.The company's Homes business remained another key growth driver, with revenue increasing 25.3% YoY. The segment added 676,000 customers during the quarter, taking its total customer base to 15.4 million.Airtel Business reported an 11.4% YoY increase in revenue, driven by broad-based growth across its core connectivity business and digital services portfolio. Digital TV revenue rose 2.4% YoY to Rs 771 crore, supported by growing adoption of IPTV services.Africa continued to deliver strong growth, with revenue increasing 25.7% YoY in reported currency and 20.6% in constant currency. The business had a customer base of 193.9 million.Airtel's balance sheet also strengthened during the quarter. Its consolidated net debt-to-EBITDA ratio, on an annualised basis, improved to 1.18 from 1.63 as of September 30, 2025. The net debt-to-EBITDAaL ratio, excluding lease obligations, stood at 0.70.The company reported consolidated capital expenditure of Rs 12,467 crore during the quarter, including Rs 9,908 crore in India. It also invested Rs 2,826 crore in a strategic land parcel for its data centre expansion plans in the country.Postpaid additions hit record; smartphone data base expandsOn the operational front, Airtel added 2.9 million smartphone data customers sequentially, taking the number of such users to 81% of its overall mobile customer base. Smartphone data customer additions stood at 18.8 million over the past year.The postpaid segment recorded net additions of 1.2 million customers during the quarter, its strongest-ever performance in a single quarter, taking the overall postpaid base to 31.2 million.Mobile data consumption increased 36.5% YoY to 36.5 GB per customer per month.The company added 497 towers and 11,684 mobile broadband base stations during the quarter. Its network expansion over the past year included 5,649 additional towers and 44,718 kilometres of fibre.Across its operations in 15 countries, Airtel's total customer base expanded to 693 million, supported by quarterly net additions of 12 million customers across India and Africa.Management commentaryCommenting on the performance, Gopal Vittal, Executive Vice Chairman of Bharti Airtel, said the company delivered another quarter of consistent growth, supported by its diversified business portfolio.He highlighted Africa's strong performance, with revenue growing 6.7% sequentially in constant currency, attributing the improvement partly to the deployment of Airtel's homegrown technology stack across markets. India business revenue also recorded healthy sequential growth of 2.7%.Vittal said the India mobile business continued to benefit from the company's portfolio premiumisation strategy and focus on acquiring quality customers. The segment recorded 3.4% sequential revenue growth, while postpaid additions touched a record 1.2 million during the quarter.He also pointed to sustained momentum in the Homes business, which added 676,000 customers, and Airtel Business, which reported 3.8% sequential revenue growth.The company's newer growth initiatives, including financial services and data centres, are also gaining traction, Vittal said. Airtel's investment in a strategic land parcel during the quarter is part of its ambition to build 1 GW of data centre capacity.He added that the company remained focused on maintaining a strong balance sheet, supported by robust cash generation and disciplined capital allocation.Bharti Airtel shares end lowerShares of Bharti Airtel ended Thursday's trading session 0.52% lower at Rs 2,056.90, compared with the previous close of Rs 2,067.60 on the NSE.During the session, the stock traded in a range of Rs 2,048-2,084.The telecom major's shares have declined nearly 3% so far this year. At the prevailing market price, Bharti Airtel had a market capitalisation of approximately Rs 12.84 lakh crore.

AI, data, cyber lead tech hiring at 30.3%
articles.summary: AI, data and cybersecurity represented 30.3% of tech hiring demand in the July–September quarter, up from 25.8% in the preceding quarter, according to a report by staffing and workforce solutions company Quess Corp.India’s global capability centres (GCCs) are directing a greater share of their technology recruitment towards specialists who can deploy AI, manage data and secure enterprise systems, the India GCC Tech Talent Landscape Q2 FY27 report said.Demand for AI, data and analytics professionals grew approximately 14% quarter-on-quarter, while that for cybersecurity and risk management roles increased approximately 12%. Both categories expanded even as overall GCC tech hiring demand declined 3.5%, reflecting continued investment in specialist capabilities within more selective workforce plans.The moderation in demand is consistent with the cyclical hiring patterns of global enterprises, where recruitment typically peaks at the beginning of the calendar year and slows towards year-end.“India’s GCC ecosystem continues to expand, but its growth is also changing the skills companies need,” said Kapil Joshi, CEO – IT staffing at Quess Corp.“As centres expand their responsibilities and explore new talent markets, companies will need to combine specialist hiring with reskilling and internal mobility. This will help them build the capabilities needed to support their growing role in global operations,” Joshi said.Technology and product GCCs recorded the highest share of postings requiring AI and GenAI skills at approximately 32%. Pharma and healthcare saw a five percentage-point increase to approximately 23%, while professional services and consulting rose four percentage points to approximately 22%. Telecom and networks, manufacturing and industrial, and BFSI recorded quarter-on-quarter declines in overall tech hiring demand of approximately 24%, 9% and 8%, respectively.The proportion of postings seeking AI and GenAI skills increased in each industry segment, showing that high-skill roles are gaining importance.Demand within advanced skill clusters also points towards the practical deployment of AI. Applied data science and model operations grew approximately 19%, while cloud security and AI-infused architecture increased approximately 21%. These roles support the deployment, monitoring and management of AI models, alongside secure cloud and enterprise infrastructure.The report estimates a 38–42% supply gap in AI, data and analytics and a 30–35% gap in cybersecurity and risk management.It identified pathways to address these shortages through transitions from adjacent roles, including data scientists moving into model operations, data engineers into applied AI, and cybersecurity analysts into cloud security. Structured reskilling and internal career pathways can complement external recruitment as AI requirements deepen across sectors.Tier-1 cities nevertheless account for approximately 87–88% of advanced-skill hiring and 84–86% of total GCC hiring demand in the country, the report said. But smaller cities are growing faster.Coimbatore stood out with approximately 30% quarter-on-quarter growth in GCC tech hiring demand, helping drive overall tier-2 growth of approximately 13%, compared with 8–10% in Q1 FY27.Among tier-1 cities, Pune was the only market to grow, recording a modest 2% increase, while all other metros saw demand decline. Hyderabad and Mumbai recorded the steepest declines among metros, at approximately 10% and 9%, respectively.India’s GCC workforce is projected to reach 2.7–2.8 million by 2030.

articles.title: SC rules 24-hour arrest deadline begins from detention, not formal arrest

The Supreme Court on Thursday ruled that the 24-hour constitutional deadline for producing an arrested person before a magistrate begins from the moment he is detained, and not from the time the police formally makes the arrest.
Holding that there can be no artificial distinction between 'arrest' and 'detention' for the purpose of Article 22(2) of the Constitution, a bench of Justices Ujjal Bhuyan and Atul S Chandurkar said any interpretation allowing the police to exclude the period of pre-arrest detention would be contrary to the constitutional mandate.
"The view that 24 hours begin only from the formal arrest is contrary to the constitutional mandate of Article 22(2) and Section 56 of the BNSS," the bench observed.
The verdict that the only period that can be excluded while computing the 24-hour deadline is the time reasonably required to travel from the place of arrest to the magistrate's court.

articles.summary: Shares of paint makers, airlines, tyre manufacturers and oil marketing companies (OMCs) rallied up to 8% on Thursday as oil prices plunged nearly 10%, falling below $100 per barrel after weeks. The decline came amid a major setback for US President Donald Trump, whose Republican Party lost control of both houses of Congress in the midterm elections.Brent crude futures slipped below the $95-per-barrel mark to trade under $94, while WTI crude futures fell below $87 on Thursday morning.The sharp decline in crude prices lifted sentiment towards companies that use oil as a key raw material, as well as airlines that have been grappling with elevated aviation fuel costs. Investors also cheered the prospect of lower input costs for paint and tyre makers, while easing crude prices could offer relief to oil marketing companies.Crude-sensitive stocks rallyAmong the airlines, IndiGo shares surged 7% to trade at Rs 5,489 apiece, while SpiceJet shares jumped around 5%. Paint-maker Asian Paints saw its shares rally nearly 7%, while those of peers Indigo Paints and Berger Paints jumped up to 5%.MRF shares rallied more than 4%, with each share gaining Rs 4,995 to trade at Rs 1.23 lakh apiece. Apollo Tyres and Balkrishna Industries shares jumped more than 8%. Oil marketing companies, including Hindustan Petroleum Corporation (HPCL), Bharat Petroleum Corporation (BPCL) and Indian Oil Corporation (IOC) saw their share prices jump up to 7%.Also read | Why is Dalal Street rallying today?Why are oil prices falling today?US President Donald Trump’s Republican party lost control over both the houses of Congress, the Senate and House of Representatives. This came after the US-Iran war spiked energy prices, with Americans beginning to feel the pinch in their pockets. In a lengthy post after the party’s election defeat, Vice President JD Vance acknowledged voter dissatisfaction over the war. He said this, along with rising cost of living and other factors may have led to voters’ dissatisfaction, which in turn led to Democrats’ sweeping victory in the midterm elections.One of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was "composition"—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win. And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic. There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up. So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we're going to shock the world? "No," he told me. "We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us."Well, that looks prophetic now. Our voters did show up. In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024. Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.  There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true. But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone. Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points. I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this. In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats. He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were:1) End the war2) Focus on cost of living/inflation3) Put America First4) Change our relationship to IsraelOur voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results. While many spent Monday attacking Rachel Campos Duffy for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, it turns out her political advice was sound. (She’s also a great person.)In the next few months, there's going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you. The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, “I told you so”: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.— JD Vance (@JDVance) November 4, 2026Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a Democrat, meanwhile pledged to bring the war to an end soon. “We are going to end the war," he said at a news conference in Washington. "We have some Republicans already who have joined us in ending the war, and the Founding Fathers had the power of the purse as one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people,” he said.This retriggered hopes for a conclusion to the Middle East conflict that has been raging since late February this year following US and Israel’s joint military strikes on Iran, killing its former supreme leader, triggering a massive surge in oil prices and rattling global stock markets.As a result, oil prices tumbled. "Markets are assessing the impact of the midterm elections to Donald Trump's next steps with the Iran war, pricing in more likelihood for the war to end," Reuters quoted June Goh, senior oil analyst at Sparta Commodities.Also read | Oil Price Today (November 5): Crude oil falls below $94 after 9% plunge on Wednesday after midterm results. More downside ahead?What lies ahead for crude sensitive stocks?With majority in both the houses with the Democrats, war-related spending approvals are likely to be trimmed and may ease off crude oil supply related challenges through the Strait of Hormuz, said  Sunny Agrawal, Head of Fundamental Research at SBI Securities. He noted that in case crude oil prices sustains below $90-100 per barrel, then the entire inflationary narrative will take back seat and this augurs well for the Indian economy and equity markets.“We believe the crude or crude derivatives and interest rate sensitive sectors are likely to be the key beneficiaries in the short to medium term. With likely recovery in rupee, FII inflows should accelerate and should be positive for large and midcaps,” the analyst further said.Disclaimer: This article has been written by Debaroti Adhikary, who is not a SEBI-registered Research Analyst or an Investment Adviser. articles.title: The midterm verdict on Trump's economy
articles.summary: Washington: President Donald Trump was publicly humbled by inflation in Tuesday's midterm elections, as rising prices provoked a blistering set of losses for Republicans in House, Senate and gubernatorial races.Most voters said that Trump's own policies had smothered growth and drove costs even higher, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of roughly 100,000 midterm voters.Also Read: Democrats vow bill to end Iran war after midterm sweepThe president's message that the fault lay with his predecessor, Democrat Joe Biden, didn't land. Americans saw prices start to climb with Trump's chaotic rash of tariffs last year, and energy costs spiked after he launched a war with Iran in February.About two-thirds of voters said Trump's own policies had fueled inflation. By contrast, only about half of 2022 midterm voters said this about Biden's policies, according to AP VoteCast.Voters in states from California to Mississippi were broadly in agreement that Trump's taxes on foreign imports have done more harm than good.The election results matched what voters had been telling pollsters for months, but Trump had campaigned with a decidedly deaf ear."I've done a great job," Trump said at one of his final midterm rallies in Iowa. "Prices are coming way down."Voters have buyer's remorse with TrumpDemocratic victories in Tuesday's midterms signaled that most voters don't believe the economy or Trump is working for them.Consumer prices are up 3.7% over the past 12 months, compared to an inflation rate of 3% when Trump began his second term. The president told reporters on Wednesday that the Iran war "drove the gasoline up a little bit short-term," but he felt the choice to fight Iran was worth it because of its push for nuclear weapons. "If I had to do it again, I'd have to do it again," he said.There is no guarantee that a House and Senate with a Democratic majority can fix an economy pestered by uncomfortably high inflation. Trump and Congress would likely need to work on a bipartisan basis, or simply keep the economy stable enough to allow the Federal Reserve to ratchet down inflation through its setting of interest rates.But voters did prefer Democrats to the status quo of a president who could govern with little to no congressional pushback from Republicans.About 9 in 10 voters said the cost of living was a "crucial" or "major" factor in their vote for Congress. And about 6 in 10 of this group backed Democratic candidates in their local House races.The economy is still growing, but AI is a source of fear instead of hopeThe underlying economy is stronger than many Americans think, with the S&P 500 stock index up more than 10% so far this year and the unemployment rate at a healthy 4.2%. Investors greeted the news of Democratic wins as a positive with stocks up on Wednesday.Still, the major driver of growth has been the buildout of artificial intelligence - a boom that Trump has actively stoked by refusing to codify more aggressive federal oversight.Voters don't share Trump's optimism about AI, which he has renamed "super intelligence" in federal documents.Instead of buying the arguments that AI would increase productivity and accelerate growth, about 6 in 10 voters said AI will do more to hurt society.The technology could displace workers as jobs get automated or it could be a financial bubble that if popped could wreak havoc on retirement savings. Despite the anxiety, only about one-quarter of voters said AI was a "crucial" factor.Wealth isn't trickling down to the middle classTech billionaires such as Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Nvidia's Jensen Huang and Elon Musk have become frequent guests of Trump, attending state dinners or jetting aboard with the president. But the growing concentration of wealth has been disconcerting for voters.Nationwide, about 7 in 10 voters said the economy favors the wealthy, while only about 3 in 10 said it's fair to everyday Americans. The wealth gap has become so extreme that even a majority of voters with a 2025 household income of $300,000 or more in the tech-heavy state of California felt the economy was tilted toward the rich.Still, a slight majority of voters across the country had a "somewhat" or "very" favorable impression of capitalism, compared to about one-third who "strongly" or "somewhat" favor socialism.But the election suggested that voters believe the government should use its heft to help reduce the cost of healthcare. About 6 in 10 said they wanted the government to play a "bigger role" in addressing medical expenses. Most voters said Trump's policies have made healthcare costs worse.Trump caught in a trap with votersHow voters felt about the overall economy generally depended on the size of their paychecks. While Trump campaigned on stats suggesting record low poverty, the working poor saw their own finances as crumbling.For those earning less than $50,000 a year, about 6 in 10 said they were worse off now than they were two years ago before Trump became president.People with higher incomes felt better about the economy, but that created a different problem for Trump. Higher-income voters were more concerned about the state of American democracy, and voters focused on democracy overwhelmingly broke for Democrats. Without congressional approval, Trump laid off thousands of federal workers, altered federal spending and imposed hundreds of billions of dollars in new tariffs that the Supreme Court earlier this year ruled were illegal.About 4 in 10 households with 2025 household incomes above $200,000 said that democracy was their top issue, putting the issue about even with the economy. Voters in most lower-income categories, on the other hand, clearly prioritized the economy.Overall, a slim majority of voters said government corruption was a crucial factor for their vote, while about half said this about high prices. Higher-income voters were much less likely than lower-income voters to see high prices as a key factor.What most voters took away from the past 22 months of Trump's presidency was that he brokered deals, took government stakes in private companies and acted in ways that put him at the center of the economy instead of America's workers.Most voters - about 6 in 10 - said Trump's priorities were misplaced.When voters were asked if Trump fought for people like them, most said he didn't.

I'm not sure that anybody's asking for a meeting," while adding that his "relationship with Kim Jong Un is very good."Trump's focus on Kim and his scaling back of joint US-South Korean military drills have alarmed Asian allies, while sparking speculation that he is seeking a foreign policy win as his war with Iran stalls.Also Read: Trump renews push for permanent daylight saving time, urges Senate to pass Sunshine Protection ActBut Kim's powerful sister Kim Yo Jong signalled on Wednesday that there was little appetite for renewed dialogue with Washington, saying Pyongyang had "no need to sit face to face with such unreliable and hostile persons"."The choice for peace includes dialogue of course, but this is not surely equated with national interests for us," she said.Kim Yo Jong's comments came after the FBI accused North Korea of a $6 billion heist from cryptocurrency exchange Binance -- allegations she had previously slammed as "a grave political provocation".Kim's statement marked "a shift from defence to offence", said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University's Institute for Far Eastern Studies in South Korea."The latest statement uses the (cyberattack) issue as an opportunity to condemn the entire US policy of pressure against North Korea," he told AFP.Also Read: Democrats' US midterm sweep may give India more room to negotiate a balanced trade deal with TrumpIn 2019, North Korea's Kim Jong Un made a 60-hour train journey home from Hanoi empty-handed after a summit with Trump collapsed.Now, the dynamic has reversed. Trump is making repeated overtures, only to be met with reluctance from Pyongyang."For Kim Jong Un, maintaining the status quo is the best option right now," Lim said.Weakened TrumpAnalysts say the North Korean leader has even less incentive to meet Trump after his Republican party suffered a thumping defeat in the US midterm elections on November 3.Voters handed control of Congress to the Democrats in a stunning rebuke to Trump, leaving him as a lame duck president for the remaining two years of his term."Trump is expected to continue pursuing top-down dialogue with North Korea", said Yang Moo-jin, former president of the South's University of North Korean Studies.But Washington's "divided government and Trump's lame-duck status will be an important variable for North Korea".Pyongyang will be sceptical of Washington's ability to deliver lasting concessions, said Michael Bosack, founding director of the Parley Policy Institute and a former UN Command official."The Kim regime is looking for substantial and durable changes in US policy towards North Korea. Right now, nothing Trump offers comes with a guarantee that it will last beyond January 2029," Bosack told AFP, referring to the date when the US president's second term ends.Kim's deepening ties with Russia and China have also strengthened his position and reduced his incentive to engage with Washington.North Korea's economy grew more than three percent for a third straight year in 2025, Seoul's central bank estimated in July, citing Pyongyang's "expansion of economic cooperation with Russia" as its major driver.Nuclear ambitionsEven if Trump and Kim agree to meet, their differences over North Korea's nuclear weapons programme remain a major obstacle to any breakthrough.Pyongyang has repeatedly made clear it is no longer prepared to discuss denuclearisation.Kim Yo Jong said in September that the country's nuclear-armed status was "absolute", calling those hoping for denuclearisation "idiots".It came as South Korea's dovish President Lee Jae Myung -- who has repeatedly offered Pyongyang talks without preconditions -- suggested Washington seek a freeze, rather than the immediate elimination, of the North's nuclear programme and offer sanctions relief in return.That approach would face significant obstacles following Trump's midterm defeat though, with Democrats committed to denuclearisation and Congress holding powers over sanctions relief."Pyongyang retains negative memories of failing to make progress in negotiations under the Biden administration because of its position that there would be no sanctions relief or dialogue without prior denuclearisation measures," Kyungnam University's Lim said.North Korea's distrust of Washington, coupled with the uncertainty surrounding any agreement with Trump, could boost its nuclear ambitions."North Korea's belief that independently advancing its nuclear arsenal, regardless of changes in US administrations or political parties, was the right and strategically sound decision will be further reinforced," Lim said.Pyongyang has carried out a flurry of weapons tests in recent weeks, including trials of cluster-bomb warheads, attack drones, a precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile."The development, testing and training of new weapons will become regular and routine activities," Lim predicted.
